displayQuote: Trust no one in whom the desire to punish is strong

meta.title: Who really said "Trust no one in whom the desire to punish is strong"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Dostoevsky never wrote it. The line is a paraphrase of Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra: “distrust all in whom the impulse to punish is powerful.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Trust no one in whom the desire to punish is strong'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Dostoevsky. It's a loose paraphrase of Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra — “distrust all in whom the impulse to punish is powerful.”

answer.label: Not Fyodor Dostoevsky — a paraphrase of Nietzsche
answer.sourceLine: Dostoevsky is not the source: Wikiquote lists this line among quotations misattributed to him ↗. The one documented origin for any variant is Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra (Part Two, “The Tarantulas,” 1883), which in Thomas Common's translation reads “distrust all in whom the impulse to punish is powerful!” The circulating “desire to punish is strong” wording is a loose paraphrase (also pinned on Goethe), not a phrase found verbatim in Dostoevsky.

source.excerpt: But thus do I counsel you, my friends: distrust all in whom the impulse to punish is powerful! They are people of bad race and lineage; out of their countenances peer the hangman and the sleuth-hound.
trail: Wikiquote lists “Trust no one in whom the desire to punish is strong” in its Fyodor Dostoyevsky — Misattributed section ↗, noting the only definite source is Nietzsche.
In Nietzsche's Thus Spake Zarathustra, “The Tarantulas” ↗, the line reads “distrust all in whom the impulse to punish is powerful!”
The same idea is also loosely floated as Goethe ↗, again unsourced — a sign of a free-floating paraphrase rather than a genuine quotation.
source.excerptNote: Nietzsche's original line, from the Thomas Common (1909) English translation. The widely shared “Trust no one in whom the desire to punish is strong” is a reworded paraphrase of this sentence.

source.rightsNote: The underlying source is public domain: Nietzsche's Also sprach Zarathustra was published in 1883, and Thomas Common's English translation in 1909 — both well before 1931. The exact “desire to punish is strong” wording, however, is an anonymous later paraphrase, not a phrase drawn verbatim from any specific in-copyright edition.

author.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
author.heading: About Friedrich Nietzsche
author.bio: Friedrich Nietzsche was a German philosopher whose work on morality, power, and ressentiment reshaped modern thought. In Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883–85) he warned against “preachers of equality” whose talk of justice masks a will to punish — the passage that later mutated into this widely shared, and widely misattributed, one-liner.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is a classic “magnet-name” misquote: a striking line about the psychology of punishment gets pinned on famous moralists it doesn't belong to.

items.why: Widely shared as Dostoevsky, but Wikiquote lists it in his Misattributed section ↗, with no work of his containing it and Nietzsche named as the real source.
Also circulated as Goethe (e.g. “Distrust those in whom the desire to punish is strong”), but it appears only in unsourced Goethe lists ↗ that themselves flag Nietzsche.

misattribution.truthLine: The one documented origin is Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra ↗: “distrust all in whom the impulse to punish is powerful!” — the “desire to punish is strong” version is a paraphrase.

context.heading: A warning about vengeance dressed as justice
lead: In “The Tarantulas,” Nietzsche has Zarathustra rail against “preachers of equality” whose demands for justice, he argues, are really disguised revenge. The counsel to “distrust all in whom the impulse to punish is powerful” sits at the heart of that critique of ressentiment.

Stripped of its context and softened into “Trust no one in whom the desire to punish is strong,” the line reads as a tidy aphorism about human character — which is exactly why it drifted onto Dostoevsky and Goethe, names that carry moral gravity.
